**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: One and Three Quarter Hours.**

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES: Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
A modern economy produces a large output of capital goods which are continually wearing out or becoming **obsolete**. Repairs and replacements are required as capital depreciates. In any one year, some proportion of the total output of producer goods is required for replacement. It could happen that the rate of **depreciation** exceeds the total output so that net investment is negative.

*Source: Introductory Economics by F.J. Grants and Stanlake pages 36-37.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define the underlined terms. (4 marks)

(ii) Differentiate between capital widening and capital deepening. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Definitions (2 marks each):**

- **Obsolete:** a capital good is obsolete when it is **out of date and no longer worth using**, because newer, more efficient machines or methods have been developed, even though it may still work physically.
- **Depreciation:** the **fall in the value of capital goods over time** (also called capital consumption) due to wear and tear, ageing and obsolescence; it is the part of the capital stock that is used up in production in a given period.

**(ii) Capital widening and capital deepening (4 marks):**

- **Capital widening** is an increase in the total capital stock in the **same proportion as the labour force**, so that each new worker is equipped with the same amount of capital as the existing workers. The **capital-labour ratio (capital per worker) stays constant**. It means more of the same capital goods.
- **Capital deepening** is an increase in the capital stock **faster than the labour force**, so that **each worker has more or better capital to work with**. The capital-labour ratio rises, which raises output per worker (labour productivity) and economic growth.

Example (hypothetical): if a farm doubles its workers and doubles its tractors, that is capital widening; if it keeps the same workers but doubles its tractors, that is capital deepening.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that the amount of capital goods produced in the economy in 2011 was worth 400 Million FCFA, with a rate of depreciation of 20%.

(i) What was the value of depreciation? (4 marks)

(ii) State two factors that cause depreciation of capital. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Depreciation = rate of depreciation $\times$ value of capital goods

$$\text{Depreciation} = \frac{20}{100} \times 400 \text{ million FCFA} = 80 \text{ million FCFA}$$

The value of depreciation was **80 million FCFA** (the capital goods that must be replaced; the remaining 320 million FCFA is the value left after depreciation).

**(ii) Two factors that cause depreciation (2 marks each, any two):**

1. **Wear and tear:** physical use of machines, vehicles and buildings reduces their capacity and value.
2. **Obsolescence:** technological progress makes existing equipment out of date.
3. **Age or passage of time**, and **lack of maintenance**.
4. **Accidents or natural destruction** (fire, floods).

questions.enonce_markdown: Outline four importance of capital in an economy. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four importances (1 mark each, any four):

1. **It raises the productivity of labour.** Workers with machines and tools produce much more than workers using only their hands.
2. **It increases output and promotes economic growth**, because a larger capital stock raises the productive capacity of the economy.
3. **It allows large-scale production, specialisation and the production of other goods.** Capital goods are used to make consumer goods, and they permit economies of scale.
4. **It creates employment** in the capital goods industries and in the firms that use the equipment.
5. **It makes technical progress possible** (new machines, equipment, infrastructure) and so raises living standards.
6. **Infrastructure capital** (roads, ports, electricity) lowers production costs and attracts investment.
